title: Quartz vs calcite: how to tell them apart
description: Compare quartz and calcite using hardness, natural surfaces and photographs. Learn which clues help, which can mislead, and when to ask an expert.

image.alt: Quartz crystal cluster with visible natural faces

body:
## Quartz and calcite: the useful differences

A clear stone with a shiny surface could be either mineral. Start with its shape and the surfaces you can already see, then use the comparison below to decide which evidence you still need. Color alone leaves too many possibilities open. If your specimen contains several different grains, first use the [rock versus mineral comparison](/comparisons/rock-vs-mineral/) to distinguish the whole rock from its mineral ingredients.

| Property | Quartz | Calcite |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Composition | Silicon dioxide, SiO₂ | Calcium carbonate, CaCO₃ |
| Mohs hardness | 7 | 3 |
| Cleavage | None | Three directions |
| Existing broken surfaces | Often curved or shell-like | Often flat, with slanted angles between faces |
| Color | Clear, white, or colored | Clear, white, or colored |

The [Minerals Education Coalition](https://mineralseducationcoalition.org/minerals-database/quartz/) lists quartz at hardness 7 and [calcite at 3](https://mineralseducationcoalition.org/minerals-database/calcite/). Those values describe resistance to scratching. They do not measure how easily a specimen will chip if you drop it.

For a closer look at one candidate, the [calcite identification guide](/guides/calcite-mineral/) explains crystal forms, cleavage and clear-specimen observations.

## Read the edges before judging the color

Put the stone on a plain sheet of paper near a window. Turn it through several angles and look along an existing broken edge. On quartz, you may see a curved depression with ripples resembling the inside of a shell. Mineralogists call this conchoidal fracture.

Calcite has cleavage: it tends to split along particular planes in its crystal structure. Several existing flat breaks may form a slanted block, called a rhombohedron. Think of a box pushed sideways rather than a cube with square corners. The [Open University explains cleavage and quartz fracture](https://www.open.edu/openlearn/mod/oucontent/view.php?id=9265&section=1.3.4) with specimen examples.

A single smooth patch is weak evidence. Look for a repeated relationship between surfaces: several parallel steps, for example, or more than one curved break. Stop if all you can see is polish. A cut or tumbled finish can hide the original texture.

![Schematic illustration of curved quartz fracture and flat calcite cleavage faces; natural specimens vary](/images/quartz-calcite-surfaces.jpg)

## A pointed crystal can still be calcite

The quartz cluster at the top of this page has recognizable points, but “pointed” does not mean “quartz.” Compare it with the calcite photograph below. This specimen has a tapered growth form known as dogtooth spar.

Keep crystal growth and breakage separate when you describe your find. A crystal face developed as the mineral grew. A cleavage face formed when it split. You may see both on one specimen. A point on one end and a flat break on the other describe different parts of its history.

For a photograph, choose an angle that shows the sides as well as the tip. A view straight down onto a point may hide the shape you need to compare. If your stone is rounded, skip the crystal-shape comparison and concentrate on any exposed natural surfaces.

![A real calcite crystal in dogtooth spar form: a pointed shape alone does not identify quartz](/images/calcite.jpg)

## What hardness can tell you

The four-step gap on the Mohs scale makes hardness useful when an examiner can test an appropriate sample. Quartz resists scratching much more than calcite. The scale ranks minerals; dividing seven by three does not give a meaningful “times harder” result.

For a loose, expendable teaching specimen, a mineral club or geology instructor can demonstrate a controlled test with reference materials. They can also show the difference between a groove in the specimen and a streak of material left by the testing object. A line that wipes away is not evidence of a scratch.

Leave jewelry, polished display pieces, and inherited specimens unmarked. A scratch test leaves damage, and a setting may prevent you from reaching the stone without touching metal or another material. For these objects, ask a gemologist which non-destructive observations are possible. You do not need to complete a home test before asking for help.

## Why white, clear, and purple can mislead

Quartz and calcite both occur in clear and white forms. Lighting adds another complication: a warm bulb can make a colorless specimen look yellow, while a dark background can exaggerate its transparency. Compare images taken under similar lighting before treating a color difference as a mineral difference.

Amethyst is a purple variety of quartz. The photograph below gives you a real example of that variety, but matching its purple shade would not establish the identity of an unknown stone. Record color as one observation alongside surface texture and shape.

![Amethyst, a purple variety of quartz; use structure as well as color when comparing a specimen](/images/amethyst.jpg)

## Make a useful photo set

Take a whole-specimen photograph first. Rest the stone on a neutral background and keep your fingers out of the area you want to inspect. Add a side view so a reviewer can judge whether a flat patch is part of a larger face or just a reflection.

Next, photograph the clearest existing edge. Tap the edge on your phone screen to focus there, and move the light or camera if glare hides it. Keep a separate image with a ruler beside the stone. A tight close-up without scale can make a tiny chip look like the main structure of the specimen.

Keep the originals. Heavy sharpening, color filters, and a bright flashlight aimed at the camera can introduce details that were not visible in person. If you change the lighting between views, note that change when you share them.

## Work through an example without forcing a name

Suppose you have a white pebble with one glossy, curved chip. “Possible quartz” is a reasonable candidate to investigate. The color adds little, while the curved surface gives you a specific feature to compare. You still have not measured hardness or ruled out other materials.

Now suppose a second specimen has several flat, parallel steps and slanted adjoining faces. Put calcite on your shortlist and photograph those relationships. Do not label every flat surface as cleavage: saw cuts and polishing also produce flat faces.

In both cases, write the observation first and the candidate second. “Curved chip; possible quartz” is easier to reassess than a confident label with no supporting notes. Our [observation sheet](/identification-checklist/) gives you space for the photographs, source of the specimen, and unanswered questions.

## Questions that come up during identification

### Can I identify either mineral from one photo?

You can often narrow the possibilities. A photo cannot establish hardness, and glare or a hidden edge may conceal the most useful clue. Share several views and say whether the specimen is natural, cut, or polished.

### What if the stone has bands?

Record the pattern before choosing between quartz and calcite. Our [agate guide](/guides/how-to-identify-agate/) explains how to examine nested bands on an exposed face. A banded appearance by itself does not establish composition.

### When should I ask an expert?

Ask when the identification affects a purchase, sale, repair, or valued collection piece. Send the photo set and any known history. An examiner can then tell you whether an in-person inspection would answer what photographs cannot.


For a purple specimen, compare [amethyst and fluorite](/comparisons/amethyst-vs-fluorite/) before using color as an identification.
answer: Quartz and calcite can both look clear, white or glassy. Their most useful reference difference is hardness: quartz is 7 on the Mohs scale, while calcite is 3. A photograph cannot measure that property, so start with observations rather than a confident name.

title: How to identify agate: clues to look for
description: Look for banding, inspect exposed surfaces and photograph your find. Use this agate identification guide to compare clues without damaging your stone.

image.alt: Banded agate with curved layers visible across its exposed face

sources.title: Minnesota Department of Natural Resources: Lake Superior agate
Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History: quartz, variety agate
Michigan EGLE: rough and polished Lake Superior agates
National Park Service: moss agate and local geology

body:
## Start with banding on an exposed face

Banded agate is a form of chalcedony, a fine-grained quartz material. The [Smithsonian’s agate specimen record](https://naturalhistory.si.edu/explore/collections/geogallery/10026355) describes its concentric color bands. In a useful view, you can follow separate layers across the stone rather than seeing just a patch of color.

Set your find under even light and turn it until you can see an exposed face. That could be a worn patch, an old chip, or a surface someone cut before you acquired it. Follow one line with your eye. Does it curve around another band? Can you trace part of a nested outline? Where does it disappear beneath the outside of the stone?

You do not need a perfect oval. A small window into the pattern may show only a few arcs. Record what you can see and leave the covered portion unknown. Breaking a stone open to settle the question can destroy a specimen you would have preferred to keep intact.

![Schematic cross-section of a banded agate, with an outer rind and nested layers; shown to explain the pattern, not as a specimen photograph](/images/agate-banding-diagram.jpg)

## Read a band instead of counting stripes

Fortification agates have nested outlines that can resemble the walls of a fort. The [Minnesota DNR’s Lake Superior agate guide](https://www.dnr.state.mn.us/education/geology/digging/agate.html) describes this pattern in regional specimens. Use it to understand the arrangement of layers, rather than expecting every agate to share the same colors.

Choose the clearest line and follow it as far as the exposed surface allows. Then check the line beside it. Similar curves running alongside one another give you more information than a single dark streak. If a line crosses the other features at a sharp angle, photograph that relationship instead of assuming it belongs to the same pattern.

A practical note might read: “Four pale arcs around a brown center; pattern visible on one side.” That description tells another person where to look. “Striped rock” leaves out the detail that made the find interesting.

## Check a thin edge for transmitted light

Hold a small flashlight behind a thin, exposed edge while looking from the other side. Keep the light out of your eyes. You are looking for light passing through the material, rather than a reflection on its surface.

The Minnesota DNR lists translucence and a waxy-looking surface among useful agate clues. A thick specimen or an opaque outer rind may prevent a useful view. Write down where light passed through, if anywhere; do not treat a dark center as a failed identification test.

Take the ordinary daylight photo before the backlit one. Backlighting can make a faint edge look dramatic and distort your impression of the whole stone. Label the second image “light behind edge” so anyone reviewing it knows how you made it.

## Compare the rough exterior with the inside

An uncut find may look much less colorful than a polished agate in a shop. Michigan’s environmental agency shows [rough and polished Lake Superior agates](https://www.michigan.gov/egle/newsroom/mi-environment/2024/07/01/egle-staffer-offers-tips-for-finding-lake-superior-agates), including rough surfaces with pits and a waxy appearance. Those examples explain why collectors inspect small openings in the exterior.

Look around the whole stone before choosing your best photograph. The interesting patch may occupy only a corner. Show that patch in a close-up, then include a wider view to establish where it sits. A reviewer should be able to connect the detail to the same object in the overview.

Leave coatings and unknown residues alone. You can make a useful first record without soaking, scraping, or chemically cleaning the stone. If it came from a collection, save its label and packaging too.

![Real banded agate reference: follow the curves across the exposed face and compare their arrangement with your own find](/images/agate.jpg)

## Sort strong clues from open questions

Use a short comparison table when the specimen looks promising but you cannot settle on a name. Fill it with observations from your stone, not properties you copied from a reference page.

| What you observe | What to record next |
| --- | --- |
| Several nested bands | Trace one band and photograph where it continues or disappears |
| A thin edge transmits light | Record the location and keep a normal-light photograph too |
| A glossy patch on a rough stone | Note whether the patch is an old chip, polish, or an unknown surface |
| A bright color with no visible pattern | Keep the color description; leave the identity open |
| Almost all of the face is covered | Record that limitation rather than guessing the hidden structure |

Suppose your pebble shows three cream-colored arcs and a translucent edge. That gives you two observations to compare with banded agate references. If you only have a smooth orange pebble, you have less evidence, even if a search result shows something with the same shade.

## Agate, quartz, and the names on shop labels

Agate and quartz are related terms, so a suggestion of “quartz” does not automatically contradict a suggestion of “agate.” The difference may be how specifically someone has described the material. Ask which visible structure supports the more specific name. Our [rock versus mineral guide](/comparisons/rock-vs-mineral/) explains the broader distinction between naming a mineral and naming a whole rock.

Also, the agate name appears in varieties that do not have the classic nested bands. The [National Park Service describes moss agate](https://home.nps.gov/agfo/learn/nature/geology.htm) as chalcedony with branching inclusions, without the characteristic banding of other agates. This guide focuses on banded specimens; it is not a checklist for every material sold under an agate name.

A shop label can tell you what the seller called a stone. Keep it as part of the history, but ask separately about identification, treatments, and origin if those details affect a purchase. A photograph of a banded surface cannot answer all three questions.

## Build a photo record someone else can use

Take these views before sending a photo to an app, mineral club, or examiner:

1. **The whole stone:** a plain background, even light, and enough space around the edges to see its outline.
2. **The clearest pattern:** a focused close-up of the bands, without fingers covering the face.
3. **A second side:** show how much of the outside remains rough or covered.
4. **Scale:** include a ruler in a separate view. Add a backlit edge photo only if it reveals something useful.

Name the images as one set so they stay together. Note whether you found, bought, or inherited the specimen, and keep the find location separate from any claimed geological origin. A stone picked up from landscaping gravel may have traveled far from where it formed.

Our [printable observation sheet](/identification-checklist/) provides a place for those notes. If the specimen is mostly clear or white with no useful banding, start with the [quartz and calcite comparison](/comparisons/quartz-vs-calcite/) to learn which surfaces to examine next.

## Before you call it an agate

Compare your shortlist with the original stone, not just the brightest photograph. Check that the banding you noticed remains visible at another angle and that you can distinguish transmitted light from glare. Keep “possible banded agate” as a working label if those observations are incomplete.

For a purchase or a valued piece, bring the specimen and the photo record to a qualified examiner. For an ordinary collecting find, a local mineral club can help you learn what the features look like in person. You will get a more useful discussion when you can point to a particular band or exposed edge.


For parallel bands or a stone sold as onyx, see [obsidian vs onyx](/comparisons/obsidian-vs-onyx/) for the distinction between chalcedony and trade names.
answer: Start by looking for a visible banding pattern on an exposed face. In fortification agates, bands can form nested outlines, rather like the walls of a fort. That pattern is a helpful starting clue, but a striped photograph alone does not confirm that a stone is agate.

title: Obsidian vs onyx: how to tell black stones apart
description: Compare obsidian and onyx, including tumbled black stones. Learn which surface clues help, what an onyx label means, and what photos cannot confirm.
answer: Obsidian is natural volcanic glass. True onyx is parallel-banded chalcedony, a form of quartz. Polished black pieces can look alike, so compare visible bands and existing edges, and check what the seller means by “onyx.”

image.alt: Real obsidian specimen with a dark glassy surface and curved broken edges

sources.title: Utah Geological Survey: onyx and banded calcite at Mount Nebo
GIA: an introduction to gem treatments
GIA Gems & Gemology: black onyx imitations, Fall 1989

body:
## Obsidian and onyx are different materials

If you have two smooth black stones and no labels, a photograph may not separate them. Both can take a glossy polish. The useful first question is whether either stone retains a feature that polishing has not removed: a visible band, a rough patch, or an old broken edge.

The [USGS describes obsidian](https://www.usgs.gov/observatories/yvo/news/yellowstones-tool-making-lava-flows) as volcanic glass produced when silica-rich lava cools rapidly. Onyx belongs to a different material group. The [Utah Geological Survey defines true onyx](https://geology.utah.gov/popular/rocks-minerals/rock-mineral-collecting-sites/onyx-mount-nebo/) as parallel-banded chalcedony, a fine-grained variety of quartz.

| Clue or question | Obsidian | Onyx |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Material | Natural volcanic glass | Chalcedony, when the name refers to true onyx |
| A useful exposed feature | Curved, shell-like broken surface | Parallel bands, when visible |
| A polished black surface | Consistent with obsidian, but not proof | Consistent with stones sold as black onyx, but not proof |
| Main source of confusion | Other glassy or polished black materials | Trade names and treatments |
| Next step for an unmarked tumble | Photograph every side and any existing edge | Look for exposed bands and ask about the material behind the label |

## Check what the onyx label means

“Onyx” on a price tag is not enough information. Some decorative stone sold as onyx or onyx marble is banded calcite. The Utah Geological Survey documents a reddish-orange and cream calcite deposit at Mount Nebo that carries that name. A carved ornament with that label therefore needs a different comparison from a chalcedony bead.

Black onyx also deserves a treatment question. GIA has documented dyed black chalcedony sold as black onyx, as well as glass imitations. Its [guide to gem treatments](https://www.gia.edu/gem-treatment?lang=en) includes dyeing of chalcedony. Treatment and material identity are separate questions: a color treatment does not tell you, by itself, whether the base material is glass or chalcedony.

Ask the seller three short questions: What is the material? Is the color treated? What supports the identification? Keep their answer with the receipt. “Black onyx bracelet” is a product description; a specific material identification gives you something you can check.

![Illustrated material names: obsidian is volcanic glass, true onyx is banded chalcedony, and onyx marble often refers to banded calcite](/images/obsidian-onyx-materials.jpg)

## Look at an existing edge, not just the shine

Turn the stone under diffuse daylight. A broad curved depression or shell-like ripple on an existing break can help you compare it with obsidian. Do not make a fresh chip to expose one. The edges of broken glassy material can be sharp, and a new break permanently changes the object.

The hero photograph shows a real obsidian specimen, not an example of every black stone you might find. Compare the broad surface and edge shape before matching color. A highlight on polished stone can look like a white band until you move the light.

To check a suspected band, turn the specimen and watch whether the line stays in the same place. A reflection shifts as the lighting changes. If a line remains visible, take a close-up and a wider view showing where it crosses the stone. The line is an observation to investigate, not an identification on its own.

## Tumbled obsidian vs onyx: why it is harder

Tumbling rounds edges and smooths the surface. The finished shape tells you about the polishing process, not necessarily the original material. Two black tumbles may have no exposed structure that a beginner can use to separate them.

Start with a comparison you can repeat. Place both stones on the same neutral background, photograph them under the same light, then turn each over. Note any banding, rough patches, or existing chips. If all you can record is “black, rounded, shiny,” leave both names open.

Do not use how cold a stone feels or its weight in your palm as a verdict. Different sizes, room temperatures, and handling times make those comparisons inconsistent. An examiner can choose measurements appropriate to the object; guessing from a hand-held impression adds confidence without adding reliable evidence.

## Bands need context too

The agate photo below shows visible banding in another chalcedony material. It is an agate reference, not an onyx specimen. Use it to practice distinguishing a pattern within the stone from glare across a polished surface.

![Banded agate reference, not onyx: the visible layers provide a comparison for observing patterns inside chalcedony](/images/agate.jpg)

Follow several lines rather than selecting one stripe. Note whether they run alongside one another, curve around a center, or disappear under the surface. Our [agate identification guide](/guides/how-to-identify-agate/) explains nested banding in more detail.

If a decorative piece appears to be banded calcite, the [quartz vs calcite guide](/comparisons/quartz-vs-calcite/) explains why material properties matter more than a similar finish. Avoid applying a property from one “onyx” reference to every object sold under the name.

## Take photos that answer the right question

For a rough stone, include an overview and a side view of the best exposed edge. For a polished stone, include the front, back, and any patch where the interior pattern remains visible. Keep a ruler in a separate photograph for scale.

For jewelry, show the whole object as well as the stone. Photograph any markings or label, but do not pry a stone from its setting. A picture through a mounting may leave important surfaces hidden; tell the person reviewing it about that limitation.

Keep the original, unfiltered photographs. Dark stones can lose detail against a black background, while direct flash can hide the surface beneath a white reflection. Move the light before editing the image to make it look clearer.

## Common questions about black onyx and obsidian

### Are obsidian and onyx the same stone?

No. Obsidian is glass; true onyx is chalcedony. Similar color and polish do not make them the same material. Check trade-name uses of onyx separately.

### Can I tell from a tumbled stone photo?

Sometimes a visible feature helps narrow the options. A uniformly black polished pebble may not show enough detail. Keep a working label such as “black polished stone” until you have stronger evidence.

### Can an app confirm whether my stone is genuine?

A photo suggestion can help you choose candidates to compare. It cannot verify every treatment, material property, or seller claim. For a purchase, appraisal, or inherited piece, take the stone and its history to a qualified gemologist.

title: Amethyst vs fluorite: identify a purple crystal
description: Compare amethyst and purple fluorite by natural crystal shape, hardness and visible details. Includes photos, a shape diagram and tips for polished stones.
answer: Amethyst is purple quartz with Mohs hardness 7; fluorite has hardness 4. Natural amethyst often shows pointed quartz crystals, while fluorite can form cubes or octahedra. A cut point or a polished purple pebble may hide those useful differences.

image.alt: Real amethyst cluster with purple crystal points

sources.title: GIA: amethyst care, hardness and stability
Minerals Education Coalition: fluorite composition and crystal forms
Oxford University Museum of Natural History: purple minerals
American Museum of Natural History: what makes a mineral

body:
## Start with the shape of the purple crystal

Put the specimen under soft daylight and look at the sides as well as the point. On an intact natural crystal, shape gives you more to compare than the precise shade of purple. The [Oxford University Museum of Natural History](https://learningzone.web.ox.ac.uk/purple-minerals) lists both amethyst and fluorite among purple minerals, alongside other candidates. Purple is a starting description, not a complete identification.

First establish whether the surface is natural, cut, or polished. A crystal cluster with points growing from a shared base is a different kind of evidence from a polished tower. A maker can cut several materials into the same decorative shape. Ask about the finish if you bought the object and cannot tell from its surface.

## Amethyst vs fluorite at a glance

| Property | Amethyst | Fluorite |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Material | Purple quartz | Calcium fluoride |
| Mohs hardness | 7 | 4 |
| Useful natural shapes | Quartz prisms with pointed terminations | Cubes and octahedra |
| Color alone | Purple does not establish identity | Purple does not establish identity |
| Cut or tumbled pieces | Natural shape may be absent | Natural shape may be absent |
| Best first photo | Point and adjoining side faces | Several adjoining faces and corners |

[GIA gives amethyst a hardness of 7](https://www.gia.edu/amethyst-care-cleaning). The [Minerals Education Coalition gives fluorite a hardness of 4](https://mineralseducationcoalition.org/minerals-database/fluorite/) and describes cubic and octahedral crystals. Fluorite can also occur without a neat visible crystal shape, so the lack of a cube does not rule it out.

![Schematic natural forms: a pointed amethyst prism, a fluorite cube, and a fluorite octahedron; drawings are not to scale](/images/amethyst-fluorite-shapes.jpg)

## Compare faces and corners in natural specimens

A cube has six square faces. An octahedron has eight triangular faces, like two four-sided pyramids joined at their bases. Turn your specimen rather than judging a single silhouette: the side view may reveal an arrangement that a top-down photograph hides.

On a possible amethyst point, look along the length of the crystal. Try to distinguish the long side faces from the faces that meet at its end. The [American Museum of Natural History’s mineral explainer](https://www.amnh.org/content/download/396659/5833944/file/hgm_3-5_reading_what_makes_a_mineral.pdf) uses crystal shape as an observable property and identifies amethyst as purple quartz.

Crowded clusters rarely look as tidy as a diagram. Neighboring crystals can hide a side, and an old break can remove the tip. Record “two square-looking adjoining faces” or “long prism with an incomplete point” rather than forcing the specimen into a perfect outline.

## Compare your find with a real fluorite specimen

The photograph below is a fluorite reference. Use it to inspect relationships between visible faces, rather than expecting your stone to match its exact color or size. A specimen’s source label identifies the reference; resemblance alone does not identify yours.

![Real fluorite specimen: examine the arrangement of faces rather than matching the exact shade of purple](/images/fluorite.jpg)

Put your own photo beside the reference and name one feature you can compare. If you cannot see the edge between two faces, take another view. If your stone has no preserved crystal faces, move to the polished-stone section instead of inventing a shape from reflections.

Color filters make this harder. A phone may brighten the purple or shift it toward blue under indoor lighting. Keep one unedited daylight photo and describe any color changes you see when you move the specimen.

## Tumbled fluorite or amethyst: what can you check?

A polished purple pebble has lost much of the evidence that makes natural crystal shapes useful. Do not count the flat-looking reflections on a rounded surface as crystal faces. They may come from the window or lamp above it.

Photograph all sides and any visible internal pattern. Record whether the color looks uniform, patchy, or divided into zones. Those observations can guide a comparison, but a purple band alone does not confirm fluorite, and a deep purple shade does not confirm amethyst.

For a cut tower, ask whether the point follows a natural crystal or was shaped during manufacture. If the seller cannot say, record the object as cut or polished with an unknown original form. This keeps the attractive finish separate from the mineral question.

## Hardness helps, but scratching is not the first step

The difference between 7 and 4 is useful in a controlled mineral examination. Mohs hardness describes resistance to scratching, not a stone’s resistance to every kind of damage. GIA also explains that the scale’s steps are uneven: seven is not a simple multiple of four.

Avoid testing a finished pendant, bracelet bead, or collectible point with a knife or another stone. Even a small test mark can damage the finish. If you have an expendable teaching sample, a mineral club can demonstrate reference-hardness testing and show how a scratch differs from a removable streak.

For a valued object, ask an examiner to choose an appropriate method. A jeweler or gemologist can also tell you whether the mounting limits access to useful surfaces. You do not need a home scratch-test result before seeking help.

## Handle an unidentified purple stone gently

Until you know the material, keep pieces separate so they do not rub against one another. Use a padded surface while you photograph them. Do not drop a specimen to compare its sound or break it to inspect the inside.

For confirmed amethyst, GIA notes that abrupt temperature changes can cause fractures and prolonged intense light can fade some color. Those cautions are another reason to avoid heat-based identification tricks. They do not turn fading, or the absence of fading, into a test for an unknown stone.

If you want to compare another quartz lookalike, our [quartz vs calcite guide](/comparisons/quartz-vs-calcite/) explains how to separate visible surface clues from properties that require an in-hand examination.

## A useful photo set for purple-crystal identification

Take a whole-specimen photo, a side view, and a close-up of the clearest natural face or existing edge. Add a ruler in one separate image. For a cluster, include its base so a reviewer can understand which points belong to the same object.

Note whether the stone was found, bought, or inherited. Keep a seller’s label with the photos, but distinguish the label from anything independently tested. Our [observation sheet](/identification-checklist/) helps keep that record together.

### Is fluorite the same as amethyst?

No. They have different compositions and hardness. Their shared purple color explains the confusion.

### Does a pointed purple tower prove amethyst?

No. A manufactured point does not preserve the same evidence as a natural crystal. Check how the object was cut and what testing supports its label.

### Can a photo app settle the identification?

Use its suggestion as a candidate. Compare the proposed mineral with your specimen’s visible form and known history. If the identification affects a purchase or repair, get an in-person examination.

title: Conglomerate rock: how to recognize pebbles cemented together
description: Learn to identify conglomerate rock by its rounded pebbles and finer matrix, compare it with breccia, and record useful clues without breaking a specimen.
answer: Conglomerate is a sedimentary rock containing rounded pieces of older rock or minerals cemented together. Look for individual pebbles held in a finer background, rather than a single smooth mineral or a loose pile of gravel. The large pieces are called clasts; the finer material between them is the matrix.
body:
## Three clues to check

Start with an existing exposed surface. You do not need to break the specimen.

1. **Find the individual pieces.** Look for pebble-sized fragments that have distinct boundaries. A ruler in the photograph helps show whether you are seeing grains or larger clasts.
2. **Look at their outlines.** Many clasts should have rounded or partly rounded edges. Do not judge the whole rock by the shape of one fragment.
3. **Examine the material between them.** Sand and finer sediment fill spaces, while mineral cement binds the material into rock. The cement may be silica, iron oxide, or calcium carbonate, as described by the Kentucky Geological Survey.

The photograph shows an example from Ohio with pale quartz pebbles in a darker background. It is one example, not a color template: conglomerate does not have to match these colors.

## Conglomerate versus breccia

Both rocks contain visible fragments of older material. The useful first distinction is the fragments' shape. Conglomerate has rounded clasts; breccia has angular ones. A mixed or strongly weathered specimen can be harder to classify, so photograph several faces rather than forcing a name from a single view.

If the surface consists mainly of much smaller sand grains, compare it with sandstone. If pebbles come apart because they were never cemented together, you may simply have loose gravel. A photograph of gravel cannot show the same evidence as an intact rock with embedded clasts.

## What the pebbles can tell you

Rounding is evidence that fragments were worn during transport. Streams and beaches can roll and abrade stones before the sediment becomes rock. Burial, compaction, and cementation are part of the broader sedimentary story explained by the National Park Service.

That story has limits. Rounded pebbles alone do not establish a rock's age, exact origin, or the distance each fragment traveled. Those questions need the surrounding geology and, often, specialist examination.

## Record a useful identification photo

Take one picture of the whole specimen and another close view showing both clasts and matrix. Include a scale, use natural light, and keep any locality information with the photographs. Record what you can see before adding an interpretation: “rounded pale pebbles in a brown matrix” is more useful than an unsupported age or formation name.

If you are comparing an individual quartz pebble with a crystal, our [quartz versus calcite guide](/comparisons/quartz-vs-calcite/) explains why mineral identification is a separate question from naming the whole rock.

title: Pumice rock: the light, bubbly volcanic rock explained
description: Recognize pumice by its frothy volcanic texture and low density. Learn which clues matter, why some pieces float, and why holes alone do not prove an identity.
answer: Pumice is a volcanic rock with a frothy texture, many gas-bubble cavities, and unusually low bulk density. A piece often looks pale and feels surprisingly light for its size. The National Park Service describes pumice as a highly vesicular pyroclastic rock with thin cavity walls, commonly of rhyolitic composition.
body:
“Vesicular” means full of cavities left by gas bubbles. “Pyroclastic” describes material fragmented during volcanic activity. These terms explain the texture more reliably than a color name does.

## Start with the texture

Look across an existing surface in good light. In typical pumice, numerous closely packed cavities leave thin walls between them. The overall effect can resemble a rigid foam. Some cavities are stretched rather than perfectly round.

Compare that observation with the weight of a similarly sized, solid-looking stone. Very low weight supports a pumice identification, but the comparison is qualitative. It does not measure density, and it cannot establish composition.

The specimen pictured here illustrates the pale, porous appearance. Do not expect every sample to have exactly the same shade, pore size, or outline.

## Does pumice always float?

Many pumice specimens float because their bulk density is low enough, and the photographed specimen's source describes floating pumice after the Krakatoa eruption. Treat floating as supporting evidence, not a definition or a required test.

A sink-or-float result on an unidentified object is not enough to name it. Materials other than pumice can be lightweight, and a photo cannot show how much water a porous specimen has taken up. There is usually no need to soak a collectible sample just to begin identifying it.

## Pumice, scoria, and obsidian

The National Park Service describes both pumice and scoria as vesicular volcanic material. Scoria is commonly associated with basaltic compositions. Hole-filled volcanic rock therefore deserves a closer look before being labeled pumice.

Obsidian offers a useful contrasting texture: it is volcanic glass, typically with smooth, glassy surfaces rather than pumice's frothy network of cavities. If your sample looks glassy and black, see our [obsidian versus onyx comparison](/comparisons/obsidian-vs-onyx/) before relying on color.

Color, cavities, and apparent weight belong together as clues. None is a universal standalone test.

## How to document a possible pumice find

Photograph the whole piece and a close-up of the cavities, with a ruler alongside it. Record the place it was found and whether it came from a natural exposure, a garden product, or a shop. That context can explain why a volcanic-looking object appears far from a volcano.

Use the description “possible pumice” while the evidence is incomplete. A clear photograph can help narrow the options, but exact volcanic composition and provenance require more than an image.

## Compare a photo with these clues

[Try Stone Identifier on iPhone or Android](/go/) for a photo-based starting point, then compare the suggestion with the visible features described here. A photo suggestion is not a conclusive specimen test.

title: Rock vs mineral: the difference, with examples you can see
description: Understand the difference between rocks and minerals using quartz, granite, conglomerate, and obsidian, then apply it to a specimen without guessing from color.
answer: A mineral is a naturally occurring solid with an ordered internal structure and a characteristic chemical composition. A rock is a geological material that may contain minerals, fragments of older rocks, or other constituents. Quartz is a mineral; granite is a rock containing several minerals. Naming a mineral grain and naming the whole rock answer different questions.
body:
## A comparison you can use

| Question | Mineral | Rock |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What are you naming? | A substance such as quartz or calcite | A geological material such as granite or conglomerate |
| Which clues help? | Crystal form, hardness, luster, and cleavage | Constituent grains, texture, layering, and geological setting |
| Must it show an obvious crystal? | No: an ordered internal structure may be too small to see | No: rocks can have very different textures |
| Does one color identify it? | No | No |

The National Park Service lists natural origin, an ordered structure, and a definite composition among the defining mineral characteristics. A crystal's visible shape can help, but polished or broken material may no longer display that shape.

## Four examples that clarify the distinction

**Quartz:** The photographed quartz specimen is a mineral example. Quartz has the composition silicon dioxide. Its varieties can have different colors, so purple amethyst and clear quartz are not different rock types simply because their colors differ.

**Granite:** Granite is a rock made predominantly of quartz and feldspar, with other minerals in smaller amounts. You may identify a quartz grain within granite without calling the entire specimen quartz.

**Conglomerate:** A [conglomerate](/guides/conglomerate-rock/) can contain rounded mineral grains and fragments of several rock types cemented together. The word describes the assembled rock, not a single mineral ingredient.

**Obsidian:** This volcanic glass is a useful reminder that a rock does not have to be a collection of obvious mineral crystals. Its glassy character is central to its description.

## Apply the distinction to your own specimen

First decide the scale of your question. Are you examining one crystal, a polished object, or a rock with many visible grains? Photograph the whole sample, then photograph the features that differ across it.

If the sample has several grain colors or textures, write separate observations for them. For example, “pale grains and dark flakes in an interlocking texture” preserves useful evidence. It does not assume every pale grain is quartz.

For a possible single mineral, compare several properties. Our [quartz versus calcite guide](/comparisons/quartz-vs-calcite/) shows why similar-looking minerals can need different checks.

## Where a photo helps—and where it stops

A photo can show color, visible grains, and some surface features. It cannot directly measure hardness or reveal an atomic structure. Start with a tentative identification, keep the original photographs, and seek additional evidence when the distinction matters.

## Compare a photo with these clues

[Try Stone Identifier on iPhone or Android](/go/) for a photo-based starting point, then compare the suggestion with the visible features described here. A photo suggestion is not a conclusive specimen test.

title: Green rocks: how to narrow down what you found
description: Green rocks are not all the same material. Compare grain size, crystal form, luster, and context using olivine, amphibole, fluorite, and green shale as examples.
answer: Green is a starting clue, not an identification. A green specimen may be an individual mineral, a rock containing green minerals, or a fine-grained rock whose ingredients are too small to distinguish by eye. Begin by describing its texture and structure before choosing a name.
body:
## First decide what you are looking at

Check whether the green material is the whole sample, individual grains within it, or only a surface coating. Then ask whether you can see distinct crystals, tiny grains, or thin layers.

Photograph the dry specimen in daylight against a neutral background. Take a second image close enough to show the texture. Keep the lighting consistent: a strong color cast makes comparisons less useful.

## Four examples worth comparing

**Olivine-bearing rock.** The National Park Service describes olivine as a green, glassy mineral containing iron and magnesium. Olivine can occur as grains in basalt and other rocks. Seeing green grains does not mean that the whole rock should be named olivine.

**Amphibole-bearing rock.** Hornblende, a common amphibole, ranges from dark green to black. Amphibole crystals can have elongated, prismatic forms. Very dark material may need good lighting before any green tone is apparent.

**Fluorite.** Fluorite occurs in several colors, including green. The paired photograph shows the same fluorite specimen in normal light on the left and UV light on the right. It illustrates why lighting belongs in an identification record; it does not mean every green crystal is fluorite. Color alone cannot distinguish it from other minerals. If purple areas are also present, our [amethyst versus fluorite comparison](/comparisons/amethyst-vs-fluorite/) explains additional features to examine.

**Green shale.** Not every green find is a prominent crystal. The Kentucky Geological Survey describes green to greenish-gray shales. Fine grain size and sheet-like splitting point toward a different identification path from a glassy crystal.

These examples are a short comparison set, not a complete catalog of green minerals.

## Build a description before using an identifier

Record three or four observations in plain language: “dark green grains in a black rock,” “translucent green crystal,” or “dull greenish-gray flakes” are useful starting descriptions. Include the specimen's size and where you found it, if known.

Look for combinations that agree. Green color with a glassy appearance suggests different candidates from green color with a fine, dull, layered texture. If the observations conflict with a suggested name, keep the identification tentative.

Do not use color to infer a gemstone's value or a collectible's authenticity. A polished surface can hide features that would otherwise help. For material with no reliable origin, a local geological collection or qualified specialist may provide a better comparison than another color photograph.

## Keep the whole rock and its grains separate

The name of a green mineral is not automatically the name of the surrounding rock. Our [quartz versus calcite guide](/comparisons/quartz-vs-calcite/) offers another example of comparing mineral properties instead of relying on appearance alone.

## Compare a photo with these clues

[Try Stone Identifier on iPhone or Android](/go/) for a photo-based starting point, then compare the suggestion with the visible features described here. A photo suggestion is not a conclusive specimen test.

title: Shale rock: fine grains, thin layers, and identification clues
description: Learn what shale looks like, why many samples split into thin sheets, and how to record grain size and layering without assuming every dark flat rock is shale.
answer: Shale is a fine-grained sedimentary rock made largely of clay minerals, often with other material mixed in. Many shales split into thin sheets. That tendency is called fissility. The combination of very fine texture and sheet-like splitting is more useful than dark color alone.
body:
The specimen pictured here is black Sunbury Shale from Ohio. It illustrates one appearance; shale can also be gray, greenish, or other colors.

## What to look for first

Examine an existing face and the edges of the sample. Are individual sand-sized grains obvious, or does the surface look uniformly fine? Are there thin, roughly parallel sheets or chips?

The Kentucky Geological Survey notes that most shales split into thin plates, while some material described as shale can break into irregular blocks. Terminology and preservation vary, so a single missing feature should prompt a closer comparison rather than an absolute rule.

Do not break a specimen just to create the textbook appearance. Existing chips, edges, and photographs of the surrounding exposure may provide the needed evidence.

## How shale forms

Shale belongs to the sedimentary group. Fine sediment accumulates and is changed into rock through burial and lithification. The National Park Service describes compaction and cementation as important parts of sedimentary rock formation.

A fine texture records the size of the material, but it does not by itself reveal a unique location or age. Naming a formation requires geological context. A loose dark chip found far from its original outcrop cannot reliably supply that history on its own.

## Avoid the “flat and black” shortcut

Several materials can be flat or dark. Before labeling a sample shale, compare its grain size, surfaces, and splitting pattern together. A rock with obvious larger sand grains follows a different path from a very fine-grained sample. A specimen showing many pebble-sized clasts is better compared with conglomerate.

Shale also contains more than clay alone. The Kentucky Geological Survey describes variable amounts of quartz, organic matter, and calcareous material. Color and behavior can therefore vary between specimens.

## Preserve the clues

Shale may weather readily, and a fragile sample can lose useful edges if handled roughly. Keep loose fragments together with a location note. Photograph the specimen before attempting cleaning, and do not assume an unidentified layered rock is suitable for prolonged soaking or vigorous scrubbing.

For an identification record, capture the whole sample, a close view of its fine surface, and a side view showing any layers. Include a scale. Describe observations such as “dark, very fine-grained, splitting into thin chips” before choosing a final name.

If you are also examining a distinct crystal in the same collection, our [quartz versus calcite guide](/comparisons/quartz-vs-calcite/) explains a mineral-level comparison. A rock name and the names of minerals within it serve different purposes.

Compare the [slate identification guide](/guides/slate-rock/) when a very fine-grained specimen has persistent flat partings. It explains how to record the differences between shale, slate and phyllite.

## Compare a photo with these clues

[Try Stone Identifier on iPhone or Android](/go/) for a photo-based starting point, then compare the suggestion with the visible features described here. A photo suggestion is not a conclusive specimen test.

title: Calcite mineral: identification, cleavage and photos
description: Identify calcite using existing cleavage surfaces, crystal forms and hardness. Compare useful clues, common lookalikes and the limits of photo identification.
answer: Calcite is calcium carbonate with Mohs hardness 3 and three cleavage directions. Repeated slanted, flat breaks help distinguish it from quartz, but color alone is unreliable. Some clear specimens show double refraction.
body:
## What is calcite?

Calcite is calcium carbonate, CaCO₃: a mineral found in many limestones, mineral veins and cave deposits. It has Mohs hardness 3 and three directions of cleavage. Those properties help identify it more reliably than its color, which varies considerably.

A white pebble is not automatically calcite. Neither is every pointed crystal quartz. Start by recording what the specimen actually shows, then compare the evidence below. If you are naming the whole rock rather than one crystal within it, first read [rock versus mineral](/comparisons/rock-vs-mineral/).

## Calcite identification at a glance

| Feature | What to look for | What it cannot establish alone |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Color | Often white or colorless; colored varieties occur | A specific color does not identify calcite |
| Luster | Often glassy on a clean surface | Quartz and other minerals may also look glassy |
| Hardness | Mohs 3 on a suitable test specimen | Hardness cannot be measured from a photograph |
| Cleavage | Repeated flat breaks in three directions, forming slanted blocks | One flat face may be a growth face or a cut surface |
| Transparency | Some pieces transmit light; clear pieces may show a doubled line | A cloudy sample may hide this effect |

The [Kansas Geological Survey's calcite reference](https://geokansas.ku.edu/calcite) documents its composition, hardness and variable colors. Use the table as a set of observations to combine, not a checklist where one match proves the name.

## Read existing breaks without breaking your crystal

Turn the specimen slowly under a lamp. Compare several existing edges. Do flat surfaces repeat with the same orientation? Do the corners make a slanted box rather than a square cube?

Calcite can break into rhombohedral fragments. A rhombohedron resembles a box pushed sideways: its faces meet at oblique angles. The [Open University's cleavage examples](https://www.open.edu/openlearn/mod/oucontent/view.php?id=9265&section=1.3.4) distinguish these internal breakage planes from crystal faces formed during growth.

An intact crystal does not need to look like a rhombohedron. Calcite has many growth forms, including tapered “dogtooth” crystals. The [Natural History Museum of Utah](https://nhmu.utah.edu/articles/what-is-calcite) illustrates several of them. Our specimen photograph shows a tapered crystal, not a demonstration of every cleavage direction. Keep a good specimen intact; use its existing surfaces and provenance first.

## Is it calcite, quartz, or a rock containing calcite?

These are different questions. An individual crystal may be calcite, while the surrounding material needs a rock name. Limestone can contain calcite crystals too small to recognize individually; the Kansas reference also describes calcite acting as cement in sandstone.

For an isolated clear or white crystal, compare [quartz and calcite](/comparisons/quartz-vs-calcite/). Quartz has Mohs hardness 7 and lacks calcite's cleavage. A photograph of a polished stone may conceal both distinctions, so an uncertain label is reasonable.

A practical observation might read: “White, glassy mineral in a darker host rock; three sets of flat breaks visible.” That is more useful than “looks like the calcite photo.” Keep the location or seller's label alongside your observations without treating either as proof.

If a brown-gray specimen remains a quartz candidate, use the [smoky quartz guide](/guides/smoky-quartz/) to compare existing breaks, natural crystal forms and the limits of color-based identification.

## What about the doubled-line test and vinegar?

Some transparent calcite produces a visible double image of a line beneath it. If you already have a loose, clear specimen with suitable surfaces, look through it at a printed line while rotating it. Failure to see doubling in a cloudy or awkwardly shaped piece does not exclude calcite. The Utah museum explains this optical effect and calcite's reaction with weak acids.

Acid reactions alter the specimen. Skip vinegar on jewelry, polished objects, valuable crystals and unknown mixed specimens. Do not treat “no obvious fizz” as a firm identification. An experienced mineralogist can select an appropriate test when observation is insufficient.

## Photograph the evidence and keep the uncertainty

Take one overall photo, a close view of the best existing edges, and a separate image with a ruler for scale. Use indirect light and keep the original files. Include any host rock rather than cropping it away.

You can [download Rock Scan](/go/) to explore a possible photo match, then compare that suggestion with the properties above. A photo match cannot measure hardness or confirm an acid reaction. For an important specimen, bring the object and its history to a mineral club or qualified specialist.

title: Slate rock identification: texture, cleavage and photos
description: Learn how to recognize slate by its fine texture and slaty cleavage. Compare shale and phyllite with a practical observation checklist and specimen photo.
answer: Slate is a very fine-grained metamorphic rock that commonly forms from mudstone or shale. Its closely spaced planar partings, called slaty cleavage, help identify it. A flat shape or gray color alone does not distinguish slate from shale or other rocks.
body:
## How to recognize slate rock

Slate is a very fine-grained metamorphic rock with a strong tendency to separate along closely spaced, flat planes called slaty cleavage. It commonly forms when mudstone or shale undergoes low-grade metamorphism. A dark color or a thin, flat shape alone does not identify it.

For a loose specimen, inspect existing broad surfaces and the edges between them. Look for a consistent planar fabric through the rock. You do not need to split it to start the comparison.

## The features that matter

The [British Geological Survey defines slate](https://webapps.bgs.ac.uk/bgsrcs/rcs_details.cfm?code=SLTE) by its compact, fine-grained texture and pronounced splitting into thin plates. Mudstone is a common starting material, although other origins occur.

| Observation | Why it helps | Limitation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Very fine texture | Individual grains may be too small to distinguish by eye | Shale can also be very fine-grained |
| Repeated flat partings | Consistent slaty cleavage is a useful structural clue | A single flat surface could be a cut face |
| Similar material across adjacent plates | Supports a pervasive fabric rather than just alternating beds | Weathering can obscure surfaces |
| Dull to modest surface reflection | Helps compare a sample with silky phyllite | Wet surfaces and lighting change the appearance |

Our reference photograph shows gray Bangor slate from Pennsylvania. Its broad surfaces are useful to examine, but the photograph is one example, not a color standard. Compare structure before trying to match its shade.

## Slate, shale and phyllite: a practical comparison

| Rock | Formation and visible clues | Useful next observation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Shale | Sedimentary mudrock that can split into thin layers | Look for sedimentary layering and read the [shale guide](/guides/shale-rock/) |
| Slate | Metamorphosed fine-grained rock with slaty cleavage | Trace repeated planar partings across more than one exposed face |
| Phyllite | Fine-grained metamorphic rock with a more noticeable silky sheen; surfaces may be wavy | Rotate a dry face under light and compare its reflection |

[MIT's introductory rock-identification lab](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/12-001-introduction-to-geology-fall-2013/7016ff5c52fad747655b3a8292ae9d6d_MIT12_001F13_Lab2_Instrctn.pdf) describes slate and phyllite using these texture and surface differences. A weathered fragment may still fall between clear examples. Record “possible slate or phyllite” if the visible evidence does not separate them.

## Slaty cleavage is not the same as sedimentary bedding

Bedding records layers laid down as sediment. Slaty cleavage develops during metamorphism as a fabric related to deformation and mineral alignment. The two structures can have different orientations.

The [Physical Geology chapter hosted by Maricopa](https://open.maricopa.edu/physicalgeology/chapter/7-2-classification-of-metamorphic-rocks/) shows how aligned minerals produce foliation and how low-grade slate differs from more visibly micaceous rocks. This distinction explains why “it splits into sheets” is only the start of identification.

On a sample with both color bands and planar partings, photograph their relationship. Do the partings run parallel to the bands, or cross them? Do not assume every stripe is a cleavage surface. If neither relationship is visible, say so rather than drawing imaginary layers onto the photo.

## Three observations to make at home

1. **View it dry.** Put the stone on a neutral background. Note whether the surface looks grainy, smooth, dull or silky before changing the light.
2. **Turn it edge-on.** Photograph the narrow edge as well as the broad face. A face-only picture can hide the repeated partings you are trying to assess.
3. **Keep the context.** Record where the specimen came from and whether it is a natural fragment, a roof tile or a landscaping product. Manufactured cuts can make many rocks look flat.

These observations preserve the specimen and make a later opinion easier to assess. Avoid breaking, sanding or drilling an unknown rock simply to create a better photograph.

## Is slate a mineral?

Slate is a rock: its name describes a material and texture rather than a single chemical compound. Tiny mineral grains make up the rock. The [rock versus mineral comparison](/comparisons/rock-vs-mineral/) explains this distinction with other examples.

If you want a starting suggestion from your photographs, [download Rock Scan](/go/) and compare the possible match with the structural clues above. A flat gray stone may still need examination in person. For uncertain or important samples, a local geology collection or mineral club can help compare actual specimens.

title: Smoky quartz identification: color, crystals and photos
description: Identify possible smoky quartz using color, crystal shape and existing breaks. Learn which clues help and why a photo cannot confirm treatment or authenticity.
answer: Smoky quartz is a gray to brown variety of quartz with Mohs hardness 7 and no cleavage. Natural crystal shape and existing fracture surfaces help narrow an identification. Color alone cannot confirm the mineral or establish its treatment history.
body:
## What is smoky quartz?

Smoky quartz is a gray to brown variety of quartz, sometimes dark enough to appear almost black. It shares quartz's Mohs hardness of 7 and lack of cleavage. The smoky color is a useful starting clue, but a brown or gray stone still needs other evidence before you label it quartz.

The [Zuhl Museum at New Mexico State University](https://digitalcommons.nmsu.edu/zuhlcollection/1411/) records smoky quartz as a brown-gray form of silicon dioxide. Use a confirmed specimen as a comparison, while allowing for differences in lighting, surface condition and shape.

## Check these features together

| Feature | What smoky quartz can show | Why this is not proof by itself |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Color | Gray, brown or very dark smoky tones | Other minerals and glass can have similar colors |
| Surface reflection | A glassy look on exposed faces or breaks | Polish can make different materials look alike |
| Crystal outline | A natural quartz crystal may have a six-sided prism and pointed termination | Cut points imitate a crystal outline; broken specimens may have no point |
| Existing breaks | Irregular or curved, shell-like fracture rather than repeated cleavage planes | Glass can also have curved fracture |
| Hardness | Mohs 7 | A photograph does not measure scratch resistance |

The [Minerals Education Coalition's quartz reference](https://mineralseducationcoalition.org/minerals-database/quartz/) lists its composition, hardness and fracture. Treat those as properties to investigate, not as measurements you have already made on your own stone.

## Start with the surface you actually have

A rough fragment, a natural crystal and a polished pebble offer different clues. Our smoky quartz photograph shows an irregular rough specimen with reflective broken surfaces. It does not show an intact six-sided crystal point, so do not try to find a point that is not there.

For a natural-looking crystal, examine the sides and termination from several angles. For a rounded pebble, describe visible color and any surviving rough patch. For a cut decorative point, record that the shape was manufactured; its outline cannot establish the original crystal form.

Keep a short observation note. For example: “Brown-gray, translucent at a thin edge, irregular shiny breaks; no repeated flat cleavage visible.” Then list the unresolved questions. That leaves room for a different identification when better evidence appears.

## How it differs from calcite and dark glass

Calcite can also look glassy, but its three cleavage directions may produce repeated slanted, flat breaks. Quartz lacks cleavage and can show curved fracture. The [Open University's specimen examples](https://www.open.edu/openlearn/mod/oucontent/view.php?id=9265&section=1.3.4) show that distinction. Our [quartz versus calcite comparison](/comparisons/quartz-vs-calcite/) provides a closer side-by-side guide.

Dark glass presents a different problem: color and a shell-like break may resemble quartz. Do not decide that a polished brown stone is genuine smoky quartz simply because it shines or has no obvious cleavage. A gemologist can examine properties that a photograph cannot capture.

Avoid scratching a finished stone or breaking a crystal to settle the question. A damaging test is especially unhelpful when you have not established which surface or material you are testing.

## Does the color show whether it was treated?

Natural radiation can create smoky coloration in suitable quartz. Irradiation can also produce that color artificially: the [ORAU Museum of Radiation and Radioactivity](https://www.orau.org/health-physics-museum/collection/lichtenberg/gemstones/quartz.html) documents a treated quartz example beside an untreated one.

Color alone therefore cannot establish a specimen's treatment history. Keep the seller's disclosure and locality information, and seek professional assessment if treatment matters to a purchase. A darker stone is not automatically more natural, more valuable or easier to identify.

## Take photos that retain the useful clues

Use indirect daylight and a plain background. Take an overall photo, a view of the best existing edge, and another with a ruler for scale. Photograph thin and thick parts under the same light so that you do not confuse a dark shadow with the stone's body color. Avoid filters that increase brown tones or contrast.

You can [download Rock Scan](/go/) to explore a possible match and choose which features to compare next. Use the suggestion as a starting point. If your sample is banded rather than uniformly smoky, the [agate identification guide](/guides/how-to-identify-agate/) may help you describe that pattern before deciding on a name.
